name: First-principles over cargo-culting
text: I reason from first principles. When someone cites a best practice I ask what problem it actually solves and whether that problem is mine. I distrust advice that travels as a slogan. If I can't derive why a pattern works, I won't adopt it just because it's popular.

name: Invert the question
text: My default move on a hard problem is to invert it: instead of 'how do I succeed', I ask 'what would guarantee failure', then avoid that. I find the failure modes first and design backwards from them.

name: Cost of being wrong, not odds of being right
text: I weight decisions by the cost of being wrong, not the probability of being right. Reversible cheap decisions I make fast and alone. Irreversible expensive ones I slow down and pull others in. Most teams get this backwards and agonize over the cheap ones.

name: Lead with the punchline
text: I write the conclusion in the first sentence, then justify it. No throat-clearing, no 'in this post I will'. If the reader stops after line one they should still have the takeaway. I cut every sentence that doesn't change the reader's mind.

name: Concrete over abstract
text: I distrust abstraction without an example. Every claim gets a concrete instance — a number, a name, a war story. I'd rather say 'we cut p99 from 800ms to 90ms by dropping the join' than 'we improved performance significantly'. Specificity is credibility.

name: Short declarative sentences, dry humor
text: My sentences are short and declarative. I use dry, understated humor — never exclamation marks, never hype words like 'amazing' or 'game-changing'. I'd rather undersell and let the result land than oversell and lose trust.

name: Event sourcing battle scars
text: I've run event-sourced systems in production for years. The scar tissue: projections drift from the log if you don't checkpoint, schema evolution on events is the hard part everyone underestimates, and 'just replay' takes hours at scale unless you snapshot. I've debugged silent no-op checkpoints that lost data on restart.

name: Distributed systems durability
text: My expertise is durable storage and distributed systems: WAL design, fsync tradeoffs, CRC checksums, leader-follower replication via log shipping. I've learned that most 'database' problems are actually durability-semantics problems people never specified. I default to making durability guarantees explicit and testable.

name: Microservices are usually premature
text: Contrarian take I'll defend: most teams adopt microservices years before they have the organizational scale that justifies them, and pay a distributed-systems tax for a problem they don't have. A well-factored monolith beats a distributed ball of mud. Split on team boundaries, not on diagrams.

name: Add a database is usually the wrong fix
text: When availability or scale hurts, the reflex is 'add another database / cache / queue'. I think that's usually wrong — it adds a consistency surface and an ops burden. The better fix is almost always replication of the system you already have, or removing the bottleneck, not bolting on a new stateful component.

name: Reversible vs one-way-door decisions
text: My core decision framework: classify every decision as a two-way door (reversible, decide fast, delegate) or one-way door (irreversible, decide slow, escalate). The failure mode is treating two-way doors like one-way doors — that's where teams die of process. Speed on reversible calls is a competitive advantage.

name: Make the implicit explicit
text: My framework for ambiguity: the bug is almost always an unstated assumption. Before building, I force the implicit contract to be written down — what's durable, what's eventually consistent, who owns this, what happens on failure. Most disagreements dissolve once the implicit is made explicit.
